name: Labradford
label: Kranky
lede: Two guys in Richmond with a pile of unloved analog synthesizers made a record so out of step that two men in Chicago started a label just to release it, and Kranky has been following that sound ever since.

eras.title: A label built for one record
eras.text: Labradford came out of Richmond, Virginia, with guitar, tape and old analog keyboards, making something darker and slower than anything around them. In Chicago, Joel Leoschke and Bruce Adams heard it and founded Kranky to put it out.

years.h: Mark Nelson and Carter Brown start Labradford in Richmond
years.p: Guitarist and singer Mark Nelson and keyboardist Carter Brown form the band in Richmond, Virginia. The early sound is dark drone rock more than ambient.
Labradford's first 7-inch comes out on the small Retro 8 label, which also puts a track on its Repugnating the Wombat compilation.

years.h: Joel Leoschke and Bruce Adams start Kranky to release Labradford
years.p: Kranky is founded in Chicago in spring 1993 with one goal: putting out Labradford's Prazision LP. Three decades later the label's roster runs from [[Godspeed You! Black Emperor|3648db01-b29d-4ab9-835c-83f6a5068fe4]] to [[Deerhunter|4f416ed7-dda2-45de-a6f1-b986e861cf4b]].
Recorded at McKinley Hall and the Belt Trade Center in Richmond, with Carter Brown on Memorymoog, Polymoog and a Roland vocoder. The Chicago Tribune called it trance rock at its finest.

eras.title: Losing the words
eras.text: With bassist Robert Donne in, Labradford dropped almost all vocals and got deeper into texture. They landed on Virgin's Isolationism compilation and did remixes, and became a band other drone musicians named as an influence, Stars of the Lid among them.

years.p: Labradford appears alongside the era's darkest ambient acts, and remixes Jim O'Rourke's "The Church Song" for Astralwerks.

years.h: A Stable Reference: Robert Donne arrives, the vocals leave
years.p: Recorded at American University in Washington, D.C., it's the first Labradford album with bassist Robert Donne as a writer, and AllMusic's Ned Raggett notes lyrics disappear from nearly every track.
Labradford gets a single out on Chapel Hill's Merge Records.

years.h: Self-titled third album, plus a split with Stars of the Lid
years.p: Labradford comes out on Kranky. The band also splits The Kahanek Incident, Vol. 3 12-inch with Austin's [[Stars of the Lid|a1154343-1ea1-4007-97d3-2382482a90cd]] on Trance Syndicate, and releases "Scenic Recovery" on UK label Duophonic.
The fourth Labradford album, its title Spanish for my better half.

eras.title: Festival of Drifting
eras.text: Labradford became curators as much as a band, hosting a traveling bill of like-minded acts. Then they cut one last album with Steve Albini, left Richmond and quietly stopped.

years.h: Mark Nelson starts Pan American on Kranky
years.p: Mark Nelson begins recording solo as [[Pan American|eeef9e6a-460b-49ca-840f-b55481b47297]], which becomes one of Kranky's longest-running projects.

years.h: Labradford's Festival of Drifting: Sigur Rós, Matmos, Pole, Robin Guthrie
years.p: Labradford launches a series of shows with Pole, Robin Guthrie, [[Matmos|46e8a8ee-d2cd-4165-9725-02f72d0027a9]], [[Papa M|6edbe0fb-734e-4b1d-9c64-73ebb04853e1]] and [[Sigur Rós|f6f2326f-6b25-4170-b89d-e235b25508e8]], and around this time tours with [[Godspeed You! Black Emperor|3648db01-b29d-4ab9-835c-83f6a5068fe4]]. A limited CD, Drifting A.F.U., is given away.

Recorded in July 2000 at Electrical Audio in Chicago with [[Steve Albini|a4d486bd-6020-4a36-9c7d-bf5ce174bcd1]], released by Blast First and Kranky. The Guardian heard Duane Eddy playing the Twin Peaks theme.

years.h: The members leave Richmond; Labradford goes silent
years.p: No breakup is announced. Robert Donne goes on to Aix Em Klemm with Stars of the Lid's [[Adam Wiltzie|fa7d8199-ba6a-448c-b25a-a615261fe6e6]], then Spokane and [[Gregor Samsa|3c651564-eb88-48e0-a862-d6db17e8464a]]. Coil had been friends who planned to collaborate with the band.

eras.title: Never broke up, never came back
eras.text: Labradford has never officially disbanded and has released nothing since 2001. Its music turned up where you'd least expect it: a prestige TV drama about a fictional pope.

years.p: Paolo Sorrentino's HBO series uses Labradford's music, fifteen years after the band's last release.
